title: Repealing the ban is a separate decision from building reactors; it removes a prohibition and commits to nothing
oneLiner: A repeal does not fund, site or approve a plant. It only stops the law from answering the question in advance.
body: Every other generation technology is assessed on its merits through planning, environmental and safety approval. Repeal would put nuclear on the same footing. Any plant would still need a proponent, finance, a site, a licence and public consent.
contextBackground: This argument tries to separate two questions the public debate usually runs together: whether the law should forbid nuclear, and whether Australia should build it. Many who oppose building reactors still accept this distinction; many who support them think it understates how much repeal would change investor behaviour.
contextDisagreement: Opponents answer that in practice repeal would be read as a signal, and that signals shape where capital and political attention go. Whether a legal change can be 'neutral' in that sense is the real dispute.

otherClaim.title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation

claimItself.title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether the 1998 prohibition on nuclear power plants should be lifted. Repeal is a separate question from whether anyone would then build one.
claimItself.body: Two federal Acts prohibit the approval of a nuclear power plant anywhere in Australia. Repealing them would allow proposals to be assessed on their merits under the ordinary environmental, safety and planning regimes. Whether a plant would then be commercially viable, or built in time to matter, is argued below.
